topics.title: The Iran war grinds into its fifth month
topics.hook: The US and Israel have been bombing Iran on and off since 28 February 2026, and by late July neither side has stopped — an exam favourite because it touches nuclear non-proliferation, oil chokepoints, and the limits of the UN Security Council.
topics.story:
The war began on 28 February 2026 when the United States and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iranian military and nuclear sites. The first strike killed Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, at a compound in Tehran — a leader who had held the post since 1989, after succeeding Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the cleric who led the 1979 revolution that turned Iran into an Islamic Republic. Khamenei's state funeral began on 3 July, his body lying in state at Tehran's Grand Mosalla, with former president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad among the mourners.

A ceasefire held from 8 April, after 40 days of fighting, but it did not last. Missile exchanges resumed in June, and by 22 July the US had carried out a twelfth consecutive night of strikes on Iranian targets. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth put the American cost of the campaign at 37.5 billion dollars. Iran has kept firing back — missiles toward the Jordanian city of Aqaba (mostly intercepted by Jordanian air defences), an attack on a border crossing with Iraq that Iranian media said killed two people, and strikes that have reportedly reached the United Arab Emirates. On the Israeli side, the war has killed 26 people and injured more than 4,290, the deadliest single strike hitting Beit Shemesh in March.

The most sensitive thread runs through the Strait of Hormuz, the twenty-mile-wide channel between Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes. Commercial vessels have been attacked near the strait, and Vice President JD Vance announced technical talks between US and Iranian officials in Doha to keep shipping moving even as the bombing continues. A strike on Iran's unfinished Darkhovin nuclear power plant, near the Iraqi border, drew scrutiny from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the Vienna-based UN body founded in 1957 that verifies compliance with the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968. Iran is an NPT signatory, and strikes on nuclear infrastructure — rather than just weapons stockpiles — raise the kind of legal questions that outlast any single ceasefire.

For India, the war has already shown up in economic data: the RBI's July policy statement flagged crude oil averaging around 110 dollars a barrel in April–May because of "lingering international conflicts," a fair description of what OPEC's third-largest producer at war does to global energy prices. India imports most of its crude and has historically balanced ties with both Iran (a Chabahar port partner) and Israel (a major defence supplier), a tightrope this war makes harder to walk.

The bigger pattern an exam might ask about is precedent: the US-Israeli logic of striking a state's nuclear programme pre-emptively echoes Israel's 1981 raid on Iraq's Osirak reactor and its 2007 strike on a Syrian reactor site, both justified as counter-proliferation. What is new here is the killing of a head of state, and the fact that the war has outlasted a formal ceasefire — a reminder, for anyone answering a passage on this, that a truce is a fact about a moment, not a guarantee about the following month.

topics.title: Monsoon Session opens with the 130th Amendment Bill back in play
topics.hook: Parliament's Monsoon Session (20 July-13 August) reopened the fight over the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, which would force a Prime Minister, Chief Minister, or minister out of office after 30 days in judicial custody — a direct test of the balance between accountability and the presumption of innocence.
topics.story:
The Monsoon Session of Parliament began on 20 July 2026 and runs to 13 August, spread over 19 sittings, with 28 bills pending. The session opened under the shadow of a bill first introduced in August 2025: the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, brought by Home Minister Amit Shah alongside two companion bills covering the Government of Union Territories and Jammu and Kashmir. Together they would require a Prime Minister, a Chief Minister, or a minister at the Centre or in a state to resign automatically if arrested and held in judicial custody for 30 consecutive days on a serious offence — one carrying a minimum five-year sentence.

The bill went to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC), which met on 17 July to finalise its report ahead of the session. Sources indicate the report will carry safeguards meant to stop the 30-day trigger being used for what critics call politically motivated arrests to dislodge inconvenient governments — since state investigative agencies and the CBI report, directly or indirectly, to the party in power at the Centre. Supporters frame it as a probity measure: a minister facing serious charges should not run a department from a jail cell. Opponents call it a tool that lets the Centre engineer the removal of an opposition Chief Minister through an arrest, before any conviction, undermining both federalism and the presumption of innocence that Article 21 case law has built up since Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978).

A constitutional amendment of this kind needs the "special majority" procedure under Article 368 — a majority of the total membership of each House, and two-thirds of members present and voting — plus ratification by half the state legislatures if it touches federal provisions, which the Union Territories and J&K companion bills likely do. That threshold is exactly why the government wants JPC buy-in before floor votes: a bill this contentious cannot pass on a simple whip.

The session's other running story is the Opposition's push for a privilege motion against Defence Minister Rajnath Singh over statements on troop losses during Operation Sindoor, India's military response earlier in the conflict cycle with Pakistan. Congress has accused the minister of misleading Parliament about casualty figures, a charge that — if a formal privilege motion is admitted by the Speaker — could force him to explain the discrepancy on the floor of the House. Privilege motions are rare and rarely succeed, but they generate exactly the kind of institutional-process question CLAT likes: who decides admissibility (the Speaker in the Lok Sabha, the Chairman in the Rajya Sabha), and what happens if a motion is upheld (the House can censure, though not remove, a minister; only a no-confidence motion does that).

Beyond the headline fights, the session's business includes the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill on higher education regulation, and a Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill — each covered elsewhere in this section, and each a reminder that a "session" is really dozens of separate legislative stories running at once, most of which never make a headline outside specialist outlets.

topics.title: RBI holds the repo rate and cuts its growth forecast
topics.hook: The Reserve Bank of India held its repo rate at 5.25% in June's policy review but cut its FY27 growth forecast to 6.6% and raised its inflation forecast to 5.1%, citing war-driven oil prices and a weak rupee — the kind of decision CLAT likes to test through numbers, not adjectives.
topics.story:
The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) met on 5 June 2026 and kept the policy repo rate — the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks — unchanged at 5.25%, maintaining a "neutral" stance. A neutral stance signals the RBI is not committed to cutting or raising rates next; it will react to data as it comes. The MPC is a six-member body created under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, 1934 (inserted by amendment in 2016), with three members from the RBI and three external appointees, and it is legally bound to keep retail inflation within a band of 2% to 6%, targeting 4%, under an inflation-targeting framework adopted in 2016.

The headline move was not the rate itself but the forecasts around it. The RBI cut its FY2026-27 GDP growth projection to 6.6% from an earlier 6.9%, breaking it down quarter by quarter: 6.6% in Q1, 6.3% in Q2, then a recovery to 6.5% and 6.8% in Q3 and Q4. At the same time it raised its CPI inflation forecast for the year to 5.1%, up from 4.6%, with core inflation (which excludes volatile food and fuel) put at 4.7%.

The RBI's own explanation ties both numbers to the same source: the Iran war. Indian basket crude oil averaged around 110 dollars a barrel in April-May 2026, well above the 70-80 dollar range that usually keeps India's import bill and current account comfortable. Higher oil prices raise transport and input costs across the economy, which is inflationary, while also widening the trade deficit, which drags on growth. Layered on top of that is a depreciating rupee, driven by foreign portfolio investors pulling out of Indian equities — net FPI equity outflows for the year have crossed 2.6 lakh crore rupees — which makes imports (including oil) even more expensive in rupee terms.

To counter the capital flight, the government paired the RBI's rate decision with fiscal sweeteners: a long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax waiver for foreign portfolio investors buying Indian government securities, alongside expanded market access for foreign investors in the bond market. The logic is straightforward — if hot money is leaving equities because of global risk aversion, make debt attractive enough to bring some of it back and support the rupee without the RBI having to burn through foreign exchange reserves defending it directly.

There is a silver lining the RBI pointed to: India's current account posted a 4.7 billion dollar surplus in April 2026, a reversal from a 4.8 billion dollar deficit the same month a year earlier, while foreign direct investment (FDI) more than doubled to 11.4 billion dollars, with net FDI of 7.4 billion dollars. FDI is patient capital that builds factories and creates jobs; FPI is capital that can leave in a week. A current account surplus plus rising FDI, even amid an FPI exodus, is the RBI's argument that the underlying economy is sound and the turbulence is imported — literally, through the price of oil — rather than homegrown.

For an exam, the useful distinction to hold onto is repo rate versus reverse repo rate (the rate at which RBI borrows from banks, always lower), and the difference between a "neutral," "accommodative," and "withdrawal of accommodation" stance — vocabulary that recurs in every RBI-related question CLAT has set in recent years.

topics.title: Cabinet clears ₹2.19 lakh crore for Semicon 2.0 and mobile manufacturing
topics.hook: The Union Cabinet approved a ₹2.19 lakh crore package on 15 July covering Semicon 2.0, a new Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme, and a National Investment Policy for Urea — the kind of scheme cluster CLAT likes to test through crore figures and ministry names.
topics.story:
On 15 July 2026 the Union Cabinet cleared seven decisions with a combined outlay of ₹2,19,353 crore, the largest single-day economic package of the year so far. The centrepiece is Semicon 2.0, a ₹1,27,500 crore follow-on to the India Semiconductor Mission that the government first launched in December 2021 with a ₹76,000 crore outlay. The original mission was built to reduce India's near-total dependence on imported chips — a vulnerability exposed by the 2021 global semiconductor shortage that stalled car and electronics production worldwide. Semicon 2.0 widens the incentive net to cover more categories of fabrication and packaging plants, chasing the same goal that has driven similar schemes in the US (the CHIPS Act, 2022) and the EU (the European Chips Act, 2023): fewer single points of failure in a supply chain concentrated in Taiwan, home to TSMC, which alone makes the majority of the world's advanced chips.

Alongside it, the Cabinet approved the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) with a ₹62,500 crore outlay running for five years, FY2026-27 to FY2030-31. This follows the earlier Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for mobile manufacturing (2020), which is widely credited with turning India from a net importer to a net exporter of mobile phones and making Apple's iPhone assembly in India (through Foxconn and Tata Electronics) a routine story rather than a novelty. MPMS is meant to extend that success toward higher-value components — displays, camera modules, semiconductors — rather than just final assembly, which captures a thin slice of a phone's total value.

A third strand, the National Investment Policy for Urea-2026, targets self-reliance in a very different kind of manufacturing: fertiliser. India imports a significant share of its urea despite being one of the largest consumers in the world, a gap that widens the subsidy bill every time global gas prices rise, since urea production is gas-intensive. The new policy is meant to draw private investment into domestic urea capacity, reducing that import dependence the way earlier PLI schemes targeted electronics and pharmaceuticals.

The Cabinet's same meeting cleared two railway projects — doubling the Paradeep-Haridaspur line (₹2,542 crore) and a fourth line between Dangoaposi and Rajkharsawan (₹1,365 crore) — both in the mineral-rich Odisha-Jharkhand belt, infrastructure that matters less for headlines than for the freight capacity that moves iron ore and coal to ports and steel plants. A week later, on 24 July, the Cabinet added a ₹3,030 crore scheme for the chemicals sector, rounding out a fortnight aimed almost entirely at manufacturing capacity across chips, phones, fertiliser, chemicals, and freight.

Taken together, the package is a case study in how "Atmanirbhar Bharat" (self-reliant India), the slogan Prime Minister Narendra Modi popularised from 2020 onward, translates into specific line items rather than a single flagship scheme — semiconductors, phones, fertiliser, and chemicals all funded separately but pointed at the same target: cutting import bills in sectors India considers strategically exposed.

topics.title: A bill to raise the Supreme Court's strength from 33 to 37 judges
topics.hook: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, listed for the Monsoon Session, would raise the sanctioned strength of Supreme Court judges — excluding the Chief Justice — from 33 to 37, the latest in a series of expansions meant to chip away at pendency.
topics.story:
Article 124 of the Constitution fixes the Supreme Court's composition but leaves the exact number of judges to Parliament, which can alter it by ordinary legislation — a simple majority, not a constitutional amendment, because the number itself is not entrenched in the Constitution's text. The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, listed for the current Monsoon Session, uses that route to raise the Court's sanctioned strength from 33 judges to 37, excluding the Chief Justice of India, who sits separately atop the roster. Including the CJI, that takes the Court from a total sanctioned strength of 34 to 38.

This is not the first such expansion. The original Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 set the strength at 10 judges plus the CJI. It has been amended repeatedly since — to 13 in 1960, 17 in 1977, 25 in 1986, 30 in 2008, and 33 in 2019 — almost always for the same stated reason: a backlog of pending cases that keeps growing faster than the Court can clear it. As of recent official data, the Supreme Court's pendency runs into the tens of thousands of cases, a number that state high courts dwarf many times over — India's judiciary overall carries a pendency in the crores across all levels, from trial courts to the Supreme Court.

The logic of adding judges to cut pendency has an obvious ceiling: benches typically sit in panels of two or three, so more judges also means the Court must generate more matching infrastructure — courtrooms, staff, case-management systems — or the addition does nothing but grow the sanctioned number on paper (a phenomenon the Court itself has flagged in earlier "vacancy" debates, since a sanctioned strength is not the same as filled seats). Judicial appointments to the Supreme Court happen through the collegium system: a group led by the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most judges recommends names to the government, following the framework the Court itself built through the Second and Third Judges Cases (1993 and 1998), interpreting Article 124 to mean the judiciary, not the executive, has the final say on judicial appointments — a doctrine that survived a direct challenge when the Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act in 2015 as unconstitutional.

The bill arrives in the same session as the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill on removing arrested ministers, giving the Monsoon Session an unusually dense concentration of judiciary-and-accountability legislation. It also lands weeks after the Court's own ruling striking down degrading bail conditions and its judgment on AI-generated case citations — a period in which the institution has been visibly active on multiple fronts at once, which is itself worth noting as an exam fact: a "quiet" court and a "busy" court are both facts a passage-writer can build a question around, and July 2026 was decidedly the latter.

topics.title: India holds the BRICS chair through a year of global turbulence
topics.hook: India took over the BRICS chairmanship on 1 January 2026 and is building toward hosting the summit in New Delhi in September — its fourth time chairing the bloc — with an energy ministers' meeting in Gurugram in June already testing the year's theme, 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability.'
topics.story:
India assumed the BRICS chairmanship on 1 January 2026, taking over from Brazil, which hosted the 17th BRICS Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 2025. This is India's fourth time chairing the grouping, after 2012, 2016, and 2021 — a fact worth holding onto, because CLAT likes to test which country chaired which year, and India's repeat appearances make it an easy trap to mix up with a different member's turn.

BRICS began as an acronym coined in 2001 by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill, grouping Brazil, Russia, India, and China as the emerging economies expected to reshape global growth; South Africa joined in 2010, turning BRIC into BRICS. The bloc expanded sharply at its 2023 Johannesburg summit, inviting Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE (Argentina was invited but declined under its new government). With Indonesia's accession, BRICS now counts 11 full members, alongside a wider circle of "partner countries." Together, the group's members account for close to half the world's population and roughly 40% of global GDP by some measures — a scale that gives the bloc leverage in debates over reforming the IMF and World Bank's voting-share structures, which BRICS members argue still overweight the G7.

India's presidency runs under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability" (BRICS), a deliberately self-referential acronym echo. The New Delhi summit is scheduled for 12-13 September 2026, but the groundwork happens in dozens of ministerial and working-group meetings through the year — India hosted the 11th BRICS Energy Ministers' Meeting in Gurugram on 25-26 June 2026, one of the sectoral tracks (alongside finance, trade, health, and agriculture ministers' meetings) that feed into the leaders' summit communique.

For India, the chairmanship is also a diplomatic balancing act. BRICS now includes Iran, at war with the US and Israel through much of 2026, and Russia, still fighting its war in Ukraine — both members India has to accommodate at the same table as it maintains a genuinely independent foreign policy line, neither joining Western sanctions regimes nor endorsing Russian or Iranian positions outright. That balancing act is itself the connective tissue linking BRICS 2026 to almost every other major foreign-policy story of the year: the Iran war, the Ukraine war's status at the NATO Ankara summit, and India's own G20 presidency memory from 2023, which set the template for how India runs a rotating multilateral chair — heavy on "Global South" framing, light on binding commitments.

A useful contrast for exam purposes: BRICS operates by consensus among members with no permanent secretariat comparable to the UN's, and its main financial institution, the New Development Bank (NDB), headquartered in Shanghai and founded in 2014, functions as BRICS's answer to the World Bank, lending to member and partner countries for infrastructure and sustainable-development projects without the conditionalities Western-led institutions are often criticised for attaching.

topics.title: Spain wins the first 48-team World Cup
topics.hook: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time to win the 2026 FIFA World Cup final on 19 July, becoming the first men's champion of the tournament's new 48-team format and the first nation to hold both the men's and women's World Cup titles at once.
topics.story:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup ran from 11 June to 19 July, jointly hosted by Canada, Mexico, and the United States — the first World Cup shared by three host nations. Mexico opened the tournament on 11 June at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, a stadium already unique for having hosted World Cup finals twice before, in 1970 and 1986. Sixteen cities across the three countries staged matches: two in Canada (Toronto, Vancouver), three in Mexico (Mexico City, Guadalajara, Monterrey), and eleven across the US, including New York/New Jersey, which hosted the final.

This was the first World Cup played with 48 teams, up from 32 — the format FIFA approved in 2017 and finally rolled out in 2026, organised into 12 groups of four, with the top two from each group plus the eight best third-place teams advancing to a round of 32. The expansion was meant to widen the tournament's reach, and it showed: Egypt reached the knockout stage for the first time in the country's history, beating Australia on penalties, a reminder that a bigger tournament changes which countries get their first taste of the later rounds.

In the final at New York/New Jersey Stadium, Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time, the winning goal scored by Ferran Torres in front of a crowd of more than 80,000. It was Spain's second World Cup title, its first coming in 2010 in South Africa. Because Spain's women's team is also the reigning World Cup champion, the win made Spain the first country in football history to hold both the men's and women's World Cup titles simultaneously — a genuinely new fact for the record books, not a recycled one.

The tournament's individual honours went elsewhere: France's Kylian Mbappé won the Golden Boot with 10 goals, becoming the first player to win the award at more than one World Cup and, with this tally, football's all-time leading World Cup goalscorer — surpassing the record Miroslav Klose had held since 2014. Attendance crossed roughly 7 million across the tournament, a new World Cup record, beating the previous mark set by the 1994 US-hosted World Cup (still, until 2026, the record for a single-host tournament).

For a CLAT aspirant, the useful frame is less "who won" than "what changed": the 48-team format, the three-nation hosting model (a precedent that could shape bids for future editions), and the way expansion can simultaneously raise the ceiling for football's traditional minnows (Egypt's first knockout appearance) while the game's traditional powers (Spain, Argentina) still met at the very top.

topics.title: Supreme Court confronts AI-hallucinated case law
topics.hook: On 2 July, the Supreme Court set aside an NCLT order built on fabricated, AI-generated legal citations — a ruling that puts India alongside a small but growing list of jurisdictions confronting what happens when lawyers or tribunals use generative AI without checking whether the cases it cites actually exist.
topics.story:
On 2 July 2026, the Supreme Court, in a case arising from an appeal against a National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) order, invalidated a tribunal ruling that relied on legal precedents which turned out not to exist — case citations generated by an AI tool that had, in the now-familiar phrase, "hallucinated" them: produced text that reads exactly like a real judgment citation, complete with plausible party names and citation numbers, but refers to nothing that was ever actually decided.

The problem is not unique to India. Courts in the United States, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere have sanctioned lawyers in the past few years for filing briefs with fake AI-generated case citations, usually because a lawyer used a general-purpose chatbot to draft a submission and did not verify the output against a real legal database before filing it. What makes the Indian case notable is that the fabricated citations reached a tribunal order itself, not merely a lawyer's submission — meaning the fabrication was not caught before it influenced, or was cited as the basis for, an actual adjudicatory decision.

The Court's holding was narrow but pointed: algorithmic tools cannot substitute for human judicial reasoning, and any decision built on citations that cannot be verified against the actual case record is void for that reason alone. The ruling does not ban the use of AI tools in legal research or drafting — no Indian court has gone that far — but it puts the burden squarely on lawyers, tribunals, and courts to verify anything an AI system produces before it becomes part of a legal record, the same due-diligence standard that already applies to any factual claim in a legal proceeding.

This sits inside a wider Indian conversation about AI governance that ran through the same month: India sent a delegation, led by Union Minister of State Kirti Vardhan Singh, to the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva (6-7 July), where India reaffirmed its "AI for All" vision — a framing that stresses inclusive, human-centric AI development with human-rights safeguards, distinct from the more restrictive, compliance-heavy approach of the European Union's AI Act (2024), which classifies AI systems by risk tier and imposes the strictest obligations on "high-risk" uses. India has so far preferred a lighter-touch, sector-specific approach — guidelines rather than a single comprehensive law — a contrast the Supreme Court's own ruling this month makes concrete: rather than a general AI statute, India is developing AI-specific legal doctrine case by case, through judgments like this one, the way common-law systems often build rules incrementally rather than through a single code.

For an aspirant, the durable takeaway is procedural, not technological: a court order or judgment is only as good as the record it is built on, and "the citation looked real" is not a defence — a principle old enough to predate AI by centuries, now being restated for a new kind of fabrication.

topics.title: One regulator to replace UGC, AICTE, and NCTE
topics.hook: The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025, which merges the UGC, AICTE, and NCTE into a single higher-education regulator, is before a Joint Parliamentary Committee and listed for the Monsoon Session 2026 — a structural reform CLAT could test through which body did what before the merger.
topics.story:
The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15 December 2025 and referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, whose work continues into the 2026 Monsoon Session. The bill proposes replacing three separate regulators with a single body — the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (roughly, "Developed India Education Foundation") — collapsing decades of fragmented higher-education oversight into one structure.

The three bodies being merged each had a distinct mandate. The University Grants Commission (UGC), established in 1956 by an Act of Parliament, funds and coordinates standards for universities and general higher education, and is the body students most associate with recognising degrees and accrediting institutions. The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), set up in 1987, regulates technical and professional education — engineering, management, pharmacy, and architecture colleges specifically. The National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), created by an Act in 1993, regulates teacher-training institutions and the B.Ed and similar programmes that produce India's school teachers. Each has run with its own approval processes, its own list of recognised institutions, and its own compliance requirements — a structure critics have long argued creates duplication for institutions that straddle categories (a university running an engineering department, for instance, answering to both UGC and AICTE) and confusion for students trying to verify a college's legitimacy.

The proposed merger follows the direction set by the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which explicitly called for a single, overarching regulatory structure for higher education — the policy's own term was the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) — while leaving accreditation, funding, and standard-setting as separate functions within that single umbrella rather than separate agencies. The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill is the legislative vehicle finally bringing that 2020 recommendation to Parliament, five years after the policy itself was released.

The bill's slow path — introduced in December 2025, still with a JPC in July 2026 — reflects the scale of interests involved: state governments (education is on the Concurrent List under the Seventh Schedule, meaning both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate on it, with Parliament's law prevailing in case of conflict under Article 254), private university lobbies, teacher-training colleges worried about losing sector-specific oversight, and technical-education bodies wary of being absorbed into a general higher-education framework built primarily around university-style institutions.

For CLAT purposes, the useful static-GK anchor is the founding years and mandates of the three bodies being replaced (UGC 1956, AICTE 1987, NCTE 1993) — precisely the kind of "match the year to the institution" fact this bill's passage into law would make obsolete, which is exactly why an exam is likely to test it while the transition is still current.

topics.title: NATO meets in Ankara as Turkey hosts for the first time since 2004
topics.hook: NATO's 32 members met in Ankara on 7-8 July 2026, Turkey's first NATO summit since Istanbul in 2004, with Secretary General Mark Rutte pressing allies on defence spending and continued support for Ukraine even as protests outside the venue were banned for nearly two weeks.
topics.story:
NATO — the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, founded in 1949 by the Washington Treaty — held its 2026 summit in Ankara, Turkey, on 7-8 July, at the Presidential Complex. It was Turkey's second time hosting a NATO summit; the first was Istanbul in 2004. All 32 member states attended at the level of head of state or government, including US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer, and French President Emmanuel Macron. Beyond the alliance's own membership, the summit drew non-NATO invitees, including Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and representatives from Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Syria — the last a notable inclusion given Syria's recent political transition and the alliance's interest in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern stability.

Secretary General Mark Rutte, the former Dutch prime minister who took over NATO's top civilian post, set three priorities for the summit: continuing to raise allied defence spending, strengthening transatlantic defence-industrial production, and sustaining support for Ukraine, still fighting Russia's invasion that began in February 2022. Several member states used the summit to announce new defence-procurement contracts, many with American manufacturers, part of a broader post-2022 trend of European rearmament that has run alongside — and been reinforced by — earlier NATO commitments to raise defence spending toward higher shares of GDP than the alliance's traditional 2% benchmark set in 2014.

The Ankara summit's security footprint was unusually heavy even by NATO standards: authorities banned demonstrations across the city from 28 June to 10 July, and Human Rights Watch reported more than 200 detentions of activists and journalists in the lead-up to the summit — a detail relevant less to the alliance's formal business than to the recurring tension between hosting high-security diplomatic events and civil-liberties guarantees, a tension CLAT passages on any major summit tend to gesture toward.

For background, NATO's founding purpose was collective defence under Article 5 of the Washington Treaty — an armed attack against one member is treated as an attack against all — conceived in 1949 as a counterweight to the Soviet Union, whose own answer, the Warsaw Pact, dissolved in 1991 alongside the USSR. NATO has since expanded eastward in multiple waves, most recently admitting Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024) after both abandoned decades of formal non-alignment following Russia's invasion of Ukraine — the single event that has done more than anything since the Cold War's end to reshape the alliance's sense of purpose.

For an exam, the summit is most useful as a hook back to older static facts: NATO's founding year and treaty, Article 5, the Warsaw Pact's dissolution, and the most recent members to join — all facts a "which of these happened before which" sequencing question could use.

topics.title: Trafficking survivors get a constitutional right to rehabilitation
topics.hook: In Prajwala v. Union of India, the Supreme Court read a constitutional right to rehabilitation into Articles 21 and 23 for trafficking survivors, ordering India's first comprehensive Victim Protection Plan with mandatory compliance deadlines — a ruling still shaping government response through July 2026.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court's judgment in Prajwala v. Union of India, delivered on 29 May 2026 by a bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan, held that survivors of human trafficking possess a constitutional right to rehabilitation — not merely rescue and prosecution of traffickers, but sustained state support afterward — grounding that right in two separate constitutional provisions read together: Article 21 (protection of life and personal liberty, which the Court has for decades interpreted expansively to include a right to live with dignity) and Article 23 (which specifically prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour, making it one of the few fundamental rights enforceable directly against private individuals, not just the state).

The case takes its name from Prajwala, a Hyderabad-based NGO that has worked on anti-trafficking rescue and rehabilitation since 1996, whose petition brought the systemic gaps in India's post-rescue support system before the Court. The judgment's practical outcome is India's first comprehensive Victim Protection Plan — a framework setting out what a state government must actually provide a trafficking survivor after rescue: safe shelter, medical and psychological care, legal aid to pursue prosecution or compensation, vocational training, and reintegration support — with the Court attaching mandatory compliance deadlines rather than leaving implementation to executive discretion, a structural choice the judiciary increasingly uses when it distrusts the executive's follow-through on its own directions.

Article 23's inclusion of trafficking sits inside a broader constitutional design: it is one of just two Fundamental Rights under the "Right against Exploitation" head (Part III of the Constitution), the other being Article 24, which bans employing children below 14 in factories, mines, or other hazardous work. Both articles trace back to the Constituent Assembly's determination to outlaw practices — bonded labour, child labour, and human trafficking — that had persisted through the colonial period and needed a specific constitutional bar, not just ordinary legislation, to signal their seriousness.

India's statutory anti-trafficking framework layers on top of this constitutional base: the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 remains the primary trafficking-specific law, though reform advocates have pushed for years for a dedicated, more comprehensive anti-trafficking statute — a Trafficking in Persons (Prevention, Protection and Rehabilitation) Bill has circulated in various forms since 2018 without becoming law, making judicial intervention like Prajwala a substitute for legislative action the Court itself has periodically nudged Parliament to complete.

For an aspirant, the useful frame is which fundamental rights are enforceable against private parties, not just the state — Article 23 is a textbook example, alongside Article 17 (abolition of untouchability) and Article 24, all part of the "Right against Exploitation," a category worth memorising as a set rather than individually, since exam questions often ask students to identify which right belongs to which category.

topics.title: India joins the WTO's Fisheries Subsidies Agreement
topics.hook: India deposited its Instrument of Acceptance for the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies on 20 July 2026, becoming the 123rd member to join a deal that bans subsidies fuelling illegal fishing and the depletion of already-overfished stocks — a rare case of a trade agreement built entirely around an environmental goal.
topics.story:
On 20 July 2026, India became a party to the World Trade Organization's Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies by depositing its Instrument of Acceptance, making it the 123rd WTO member to formally join the deal. The agreement was adopted by consensus at the WTO's 12th Ministerial Conference (MC12) in Geneva in June 2022 — itself a notable moment, since WTO negotiations on this subject had dragged on for more than two decades without resolution, making its eventual adoption one of the organisation's few multilateral successes in recent years.

The agreement targets three specific categories of harmful fishing subsidy: those that support illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing; those that support fishing of stocks that are already overfished; and those that support fishing on the unregulated high seas, beyond any coastal state's jurisdiction or a regional fisheries body's control. The underlying problem the deal addresses is straightforward — many governments subsidise fuel, boats, and gear for their fishing fleets, and those subsidies, multiplied across the world's major fishing nations, have been a major driver of overfishing, since subsidised fleets keep fishing depleted stocks at a scale the market alone would not sustain.

For the agreement to enter into force, two-thirds of the WTO's members must deposit their instruments of acceptance — a threshold under Article X of the Marrakesh Agreement (the 1994 treaty that created the WTO itself), which governs how amendments and new agreements attached to the WTO's legal framework take effect. India's acceptance, as the 123rd member to ratify, moves the agreement further past that two-thirds threshold, a milestone reached gradually since 2022 as individual member states worked the agreement through their own domestic ratification processes — in India's case, involving consultations with the fisheries and coastal-livelihoods ministries given the direct stake of India's traditional fishing communities.

India's own negotiating position through the original talks focused on protecting subsidies for small-scale and artisanal fishers — the millions of Indians who fish from small boats along the coastline for subsistence and local markets — distinguishing them from the large industrial fleets the agreement is really aimed at. That distinction (small-scale versus industrial subsidies) is the same fault line that runs through most global fisheries and agriculture negotiations, echoing debates India has separately had at the WTO over agricultural subsidies and public food stockholding, where India has long argued that developed countries' historical overfishing and over-farming should not be met with rules that penalise developing countries just as they try to support their own rural livelihoods.

The WTO itself, headquartered in Geneva, was established on 1 January 1995, succeeding the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947 — a lineage worth keeping straight, since GATT was a multilateral treaty administered ad hoc, while the WTO is a permanent institution with a dispute-settlement mechanism, a distinction CLAT has tested before.

topics.title: Supreme Court calls degrading bail conditions 'abhorrent'
topics.hook: A bench led by CJI Surya Kant struck down bail conditions that required accused persons to perform degrading tasks like cleaning police stations, calling such conditions 'abhorrent' and 'unknown to law' — a ruling that ties bail jurisprudence firmly to Article 21's dignity guarantee.
topics.story:
In a July 2026 ruling (2026 SCC OnLine SC 809), a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi struck down bail conditions that lower courts had imposed requiring accused persons to perform demeaning tasks — such as cleaning police stations — before release. The Court called such conditions "abhorrent" and "unknown to law," holding they violate the dignity protections embedded in Article 21's guarantee of life and personal liberty.

Bail conditions are meant to ensure an accused person appears for trial and does not tamper with evidence or witnesses — not to punish someone who has not been convicted of anything. Indian courts have periodically had to correct lower-court practices that blur this line, treating bail as an opportunity to extract informal punishment. This ruling adds to a body of Article 21 jurisprudence running back to Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which established that any procedure depriving a person of liberty must be fair, just, and reasonable — not merely lawful in a narrow, technical sense.

The judgment lands alongside a busy month for the Court, which in the same period ruled on AI-generated case law and on trafficking survivors' rehabilitation rights — a reminder that a single month's Supreme Court output usually spans criminal procedure, constitutional rights, and administrative law simultaneously, not one theme at a time.

topics.story:
A parliamentary "privilege motion" is a formal complaint that a member has been denied their parliamentary privileges, or that someone (often a minister) has committed a "breach of privilege" — commonly, by making a statement to the House later shown to be false or misleading. Admissibility rests with the presiding officer — the Speaker in the Lok Sabha, the Chairman in the Rajya Sabha — who can refer the matter to the Privileges Committee for investigation. Unlike a no-confidence motion, a successful privilege motion cannot remove a minister from office; its outcomes are typically a formal censure or a mandated correction to the parliamentary record, making it a reputational rather than existential threat to the government, though a politically damaging one in an election-adjacent news cycle.

topics.title: FCRA amendment softens penalties, tightens oversight
topics.hook: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 cuts the maximum jail term for FCRA lapses from five years to one, while adding an oversight framework for what happens to an organisation's assets when its FCRA registration lapses.
topics.story:
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1971 (FCRA) — substantially rewritten in 2010 and again tightened in 2020 — regulates how Indian individuals, associations, and NGOs can receive foreign donations, requiring registration and routing all foreign contributions through a designated bank account. The 2026 amendment bill, listed for the Monsoon Session, does two things: it reduces the maximum imprisonment for FCRA violations from five years to one, easing what critics had called disproportionately harsh criminal penalties for often-technical compliance failures, while simultaneously creating a clearer legal framework for what happens to an organisation's foreign-funded assets once its FCRA registration lapses or is cancelled — previously an area of legal ambiguity that left assets in limbo.

FCRA registration has been a recurring flashpoint in India's civil-society sector, with rights groups arguing the 2020 tightening was used to restrict foreign funding to organisations critical of government policy, while the government maintains the law is a legitimate national-security and financial-transparency tool, consistent with similar foreign-agent registration laws in other democracies.

He is remembered as cricket's finest all-rounder — equally capable with bat, in three different bowling styles, and in the field — and captained the West Indies during the 1960s and 1970s, an era in which the team was already establishing the dominance it would sustain into the 1980s. His 365 not out against Pakistan in 1958 stood as the highest individual score in Test cricket for 36 years, until Brian Lara broke it in 1994. Sobers was knighted in 1975 for his services to cricket.

facts.v: 365 not out (1958), highest Test score for 36 years

topics.why: Obituary facts on iconic sportspeople are a reliable CLAT staple — the record-and-year-broken pairing (Sobers 1958 / Lara 1994) is the likely test angle.

passages.title: A ceasefire that did not hold
passages.passage:
The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran began on 28 February 2026 with coordinated strikes that killed Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, at a compound in Tehran. A ceasefire took effect on 8 April, after 40 days of fighting, and for a while it appeared the conflict had burned through its worst phase. Diplomats spoke of technical talks, of shipping lanes reopening through the Strait of Hormuz, of a region exhausted enough to want a pause to last.

It did not last. Missile exchanges resumed in June, and by late July the United States had carried out a twelfth consecutive night of strikes on Iranian targets, with the American Defense Secretary putting the campaign's cost at 37.5 billion dollars. Iran has kept firing back — toward Jordan, toward a border crossing with Iraq, reportedly toward the United Arab Emirates — while a strike on an unfinished Iranian nuclear power plant near the Iraqi border drew the International Atomic Energy Agency into an investigation of its own.

For India, the war has shown up less as a headline and more as a line item. The Reserve Bank of India's June policy statement cited Indian-basket crude oil averaging around 110 dollars a barrel in April and May, well above the range that keeps India's import bill comfortable, and tied part of its decision to raise its inflation forecast directly to "lingering international conflicts." A war fought thousands of kilometres from Mumbai still finds its way into the price of a scooter's petrol tank, because India imports most of the oil it burns, and Iran's neighbourhood happens to sit on top of a fifth of the world's seaborne oil trade.

What the April ceasefire mainly proved is that a truce is a fact about the day it is signed, not a guarantee about the months after. Reading the war's progress by counting days since the last ceasefire, rather than days since the war began, has become the only honest way to describe where things stand.

questions.q: Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: India's economy is more exposed to Middle Eastern wars than most people assume.
A ceasefire in the Iran war broke down, and the conflict's effects have reached beyond the immediate combatants, including India's economy.
The Strait of Hormuz is the most important chokepoint in global oil trade.
The IAEA has failed to prevent strikes on Iranian nuclear infrastructure.
questions.explain: The passage's arc is the ceasefire's collapse and the war's spillover, using India's inflation forecast as one concrete example — not its central claim. Option A overstates a supporting detail as if it were the thesis; C and D pick out true but secondary facts.

questions.q: Based on the passage, what can be inferred about the RBI's reasoning in raising its inflation forecast?
options: The RBI blamed the rupee's depreciation entirely on domestic banking policy.
The RBI considered the Iran war's effect on oil prices to be a contributing factor to inflation, not the sole cause.
The RBI expected the war to end before its forecast period began.
The RBI's forecast was unrelated to any external conflict.
questions.explain: The passage says the RBI 'tied part of its decision' to the conflict — a partial, not exclusive, causal claim. Option A introduces a detail (rupee, banking policy) the passage never raises in this context; C and D contradict the text directly.

questions.q: According to the passage, how long did the ceasefire that began on 8 April last before fighting resumed?
options: It never actually took effect.
About two months, until fighting resumed in June.
It held until the end of July.
40 days, matching the length of the initial fighting.
questions.explain: The ceasefire began 8 April and the passage states missile exchanges resumed in June — roughly two months. Option D confuses the ceasefire's duration with the 40-day length of the fighting that preceded it, a classic number-swap trap.

questions.q: Which statement about the Strait of Hormuz is TRUE based on the passage?
options: It carries about a fifth of the world's seaborne oil trade.
It has been fully closed to shipping since February 2026.
It lies entirely within Iranian territorial waters.
The IAEA has jurisdiction over shipping through it.
questions.explain: The passage states Iran's neighbourhood 'sits on top of a fifth of the world's seaborne oil trade,' directly supporting option A. The other options assert facts (full closure, sole territorial control, IAEA jurisdiction over shipping) the passage never makes.

questions.q: Iran's Supreme Leader who was killed at the war's outset succeeded which earlier leader in that post?
options: Mahmoud Ahmadinejad
Reza Shah Pahlavi
Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini
Hassan Rouhani
questions.explain: This requires outside static knowledge: Ali Khamenei succeeded Ayatollah Khomeini, leader of the 1979 Iranian Revolution, as Supreme Leader in 1989. Ahmadinejad and Rouhani were Iranian presidents, a different office; Reza Shah Pahlavi belonged to the monarchy Khomeini's revolution overthrew.

passages.title: A crowded Monsoon Session
passages.passage:
Parliament's Monsoon Session opened on 20 July 2026 and runs to 13 August, with 28 bills pending across its 19 sittings. The bill drawing the most attention is not new: the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, introduced in August 2025, which would require a Prime Minister, Chief Minister, or minister to resign automatically after 30 consecutive days in judicial custody for a serious offence. A Joint Parliamentary Committee finalised its report on the bill on 17 July, reportedly adding safeguards meant to stop the 30-day trigger from being used to engineer the removal of an inconvenient state government before any conviction is secured.

The bill needs the special majority procedure that any constitutional amendment requires — a majority of each House's total membership, and two-thirds of those present and voting — plus ratification by half the state legislatures where it touches federal arrangements, since its companion bills extend the same rule to Union Territory administrations and Jammu and Kashmir. That threshold is precisely why the government sought the JPC's endorsement before bringing the bill to a floor vote: legislation this contentious rarely survives on a party's own numbers alone.

The same session carries a second, quieter judiciary bill: a proposal to raise the Supreme Court's sanctioned strength from 33 judges to 37, excluding the Chief Justice. Unlike the 130th Amendment, this bill does not touch the Constitution's text directly — the number of judges has always been left to ordinary parliamentary legislation, amendable by a simple majority, which is why it has been revised upward five times since the Supreme Court's original 1956 strength of ten judges plus the Chief Justice.

Two bills, then, moving through the same session, aimed at two different institutions, but both testing the same underlying question a passage-writer might ask: which changes to the machinery of Indian government require the Constitution's heaviest procedural bar, and which can pass through Parliament's ordinary front door.

questions.q: What is the central contrast the passage draws between the two bills discussed?
options: One bill concerns the judiciary and the other the executive, with no procedural difference between them.
The 130th Amendment Bill requires a constitutional amendment's special majority and state ratification, while the Supreme Court judges bill can pass by ordinary legislation.
Both bills require a two-thirds majority in both Houses.
The Supreme Court judges bill is more contentious than the 130th Amendment Bill.
questions.explain: The passage's final paragraph makes this contrast explicit. Option C is false — only the 130th Amendment needs the special majority; option D inverts the passage's own framing, which treats the 130th Amendment as the more contentious bill.

questions.q: Why, based on the passage, did the government seek the JPC's endorsement before a floor vote on the 130th Amendment Bill?
options: Because JPC endorsement is legally required for every constitutional amendment.
Because the bill's high procedural threshold means it is unlikely to pass without broader political buy-in the JPC process can help build.
Because the Supreme Court ordered a JPC review before the bill could be introduced.
Because the JPC has the power to reject bills outright.
questions.explain: The passage says the special-majority threshold 'is precisely why' the JPC route was sought, implying a strategic, not a strictly legal, reason. Option A overstates JPC review as a universal legal requirement, which the passage never claims.

questions.q: According to the passage, which of these statements is FALSE?
options: The 130th Amendment Bill was introduced in August 2025.
The Supreme Court judges bill would raise the strength to 37, including the Chief Justice.
The Monsoon Session has 28 pending bills.
The JPC finalised its report on 17 July 2026.
questions.explain: The passage explicitly says the increase to 37 is 'excluding the Chief Justice' — option B inverts this, making it the false statement the question asks for. The other three options restate facts directly given in the text.

questions.q: The passage implies that constitutional amendments touching 'federal arrangements' require which additional step beyond a special majority in Parliament?
options: Approval by the Supreme Court
A national referendum
Ratification by half the state legislatures
Presidential assent given twice
questions.explain: The passage states such amendments need 'ratification by half the state legislatures.' The other options describe procedures India's amendment process does not use at all.

questions.q: The original strength of the Supreme Court under the 1956 Act, referenced in the passage, is most comparable in spirit to which other constitutional design choice left to ordinary parliamentary law rather than the Constitution's text?
options: The territorial extent of India's Union Territories
The qualifications for Presidential candidacy
The number of judges in a state High Court, similarly set by ordinary statute
The tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner
questions.explain: This requires outside knowledge: like the Supreme Court, the strength of each High Court is fixed by the President under ordinary law (Article 216 read with relevant statutes), not the Constitution's text — a genuine parallel. Presidential qualifications and Union Territory boundaries are constitutionally or specifically statutorily defined in different, non-analogous ways.

passages.title: Holding steady, revising everything else
passages.passage:
When the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee met on 5 June 2026, the headline decision was almost anticlimactic: the repo rate stayed exactly where it was, at 5.25 percent, with the Committee maintaining what it calls a "neutral" stance — a way of signalling that it is not committed to cutting or raising rates next, only to reacting as new data arrives. Reading only the rate decision, one might conclude the RBI saw a quiet quarter ahead.

The forecasts attached to that decision tell a different story. The Committee cut its growth projection for the current financial year to 6.6 percent, down from an earlier 6.9 percent, while raising its inflation forecast to 5.1 percent from 4.6 percent. Both revisions point the same way: toward an economy absorbing higher costs. The RBI's own explanation names the source directly — crude oil, averaging around 110 dollars a barrel through April and May, a price shaped by conflicts far from India's borders but felt immediately in the cost of transporting nearly everything the country buys and sells.

A weakening rupee compounded the problem. Foreign portfolio investors pulled more than 2.6 lakh crore rupees out of Indian equities over the year, and every rupee that leaves puts pressure on the exchange rate, making imported oil more expensive in rupee terms even before global prices move. The government's response was not to ask the RBI to raise rates and defend the currency directly, but to make Indian government bonds more attractive to foreign money — waiving long-term capital gains tax for foreign investors buying government securities, hoping to draw back through the debt market what equities were losing.

There was a genuine bright spot buried in the same data: India's current account swung to a surplus in April 2026, and foreign direct investment more than doubled year on year. FDI builds factories; FPI can leave within a week of a bad headline. The RBI's message, taken as a whole, was less "nothing changed" than "the ground shifted, and we are choosing not to chase it with the blunt tool of interest rates just yet."

questions.q: What is the main idea the passage develops across its four paragraphs?
options: The RBI's decision to hold the repo rate was straightforward and required no further explanation.
Beneath an unchanged headline rate, the RBI's growth and inflation forecasts, and its accompanying fiscal measures, reveal significant underlying economic strain.
Foreign portfolio investors are solely responsible for India's economic troubles in 2026.
India's current account surplus proves the economy faced no real difficulty in mid-2026.
questions.explain: The passage's structure — 'anticlimactic' rate decision followed by three paragraphs of underlying strain — supports option B. Option D contradicts the passage's own framing of the surplus as one bright spot amid genuine difficulty, not proof of an absence of trouble.

questions.q: What can be inferred about why the government chose an LTCG waiver rather than asking the RBI to raise rates to defend the rupee?
options: The RBI does not have the legal authority to raise interest rates.
The government preferred to address capital flight by making debt investment more attractive, rather than tightening monetary policy that could further slow growth already under pressure.
LTCG waivers are required by international trade law during a currency crisis.
The rupee was not actually depreciating.
questions.explain: The passage sets up growth already under pressure from oil prices; raising rates further would compound that. The fiscal tool (LTCG waiver) sidesteps this trade-off — a reasonable inference the passage supports without stating it outright. Option A is factually wrong and unsupported.

questions.q: According to the passage, which of the following did the RBI's June 2026 review NOT do?
options: Keep the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%
Cut the FY27 growth forecast
Raise the FY27 inflation forecast
Move to an 'accommodative' stance from a 'neutral' one
questions.explain: The passage states the Committee maintained a 'neutral' stance throughout — it did not shift to 'accommodative.' The other three options are directly confirmed in the text.

questions.q: Based on the passage's closing distinction, why does the author consider FDI more valuable to India than FPI during this period?
options: FDI is taxed at a lower rate than FPI.
FDI represents durable investment in productive assets, while FPI can be withdrawn quickly, as happened during this period.
FDI does not require RBI approval, unlike FPI.
FPI is illegal under current Indian law.
questions.explain: The passage explicitly contrasts 'FDI builds factories; FPI can leave within a week of a bad headline' — this is the stated basis for valuing FDI's stability over FPI's volatility. The other options are not supported anywhere in the passage.

questions.q: The RBI's inflation target framework, referenced implicitly through its forecasting mandate, sets what target band for CPI inflation, and since which year?
options: 2-6%, targeting 4%, since 2016
0-3%, targeting 2%, since 1991
3-7%, targeting 5%, since 2008
There is no formal target band; the RBI sets forecasts at its discretion
questions.explain: This draws on outside static knowledge: India adopted a formal flexible inflation-targeting framework in 2016, with a 2-6% band targeting 4% CPI inflation. The passage gestures at this framework by discussing inflation forecasts without stating the target band explicitly.

passages.title: When the citation does not exist
passages.passage:
On 2 July 2026, the Supreme Court set aside a tribunal order built, in part, on legal precedents that did not exist. The case involved an appeal against a National Company Law Tribunal ruling that cited earlier judgments — complete with plausible-sounding party names and citation numbers — none of which corresponded to any decision actually handed down. The citations had been generated by an artificial intelligence tool and never verified against a real legal database before making their way into an official order.

This particular failure has a name now familiar well beyond courtrooms: hallucination, the tendency of generative AI systems to produce confident, coherent-sounding output that has no basis in fact. Courts elsewhere have confronted versions of the same problem — lawyers in the United States and the United Kingdom have been sanctioned in recent years for filing briefs built on fabricated AI-generated case law. What set the Indian case apart was that the fabrication reached the tribunal's own order, not merely a lawyer's submission awaiting a judge's scrutiny.

The Supreme Court's ruling did not ban the use of AI tools in legal work. It held something narrower: that algorithmic tools cannot substitute for human judicial reasoning, and that any decision resting on citations no one has checked against the actual case record cannot stand. The burden of verification, the Court implied, sits exactly where it always has — with the lawyer, the tribunal, or the court that puts a claim into the record, whatever tool helped draft it.

The ruling arrived in a month when India was also sending a delegation to the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva, where officials described India's preference for guidelines over a single comprehensive AI law, a lighter regulatory touch than the European Union has chosen. Read together, the two stories suggest India is building its AI-era legal rules the way common-law systems often do: case by case, through judgments like this one, rather than through one sweeping statute passed all at once.

questions.q: What is the main point the passage makes about the Supreme Court's July 2026 ruling?
options: The Court banned all use of artificial intelligence in Indian legal proceedings.
The Court held that AI-generated content must be verified before being relied upon, without prohibiting AI tools outright.
The Court found the NCLT tribunal had acted in good faith and imposed no penalty.
The Court ruled that only foreign AI companies could be held liable for hallucinated citations.
questions.explain: The passage explicitly says the ruling 'did not ban' AI tools but held that unverified citations cannot stand — option B captures this precisely. Option A directly contradicts the text.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest by noting the Indian case was different because 'the fabrication reached the tribunal's own order'?
options: That Indian tribunals are less careful than foreign courts in general.
That the failure here was more serious because it affected an actual adjudicatory decision, not just an unreviewed submission awaiting scrutiny.
That the tribunal deliberately fabricated the citations.
That only tribunals, not courts, can be affected by AI hallucination.
questions.explain: The passage frames this contrast — a lawyer's submission (still subject to review) versus a tribunal's actual order — as a matter of severity, not intent or general competence. Option C is unsupported; nothing suggests deliberate fabrication by the tribunal itself.

questions.q: According to the passage, which statement about the sanctioning of lawyers for AI-generated citations is TRUE?
options: It has occurred only in India.
It has occurred in the United States and the United Kingdom in recent years, in addition to the Indian case.
No country has ever sanctioned a lawyer for this reason.
The Indian Supreme Court sanctioned the lawyers involved in this specific case.
questions.explain: The passage states courts in the 'United States and the United Kingdom have been sanctioned in recent years' for this reason — confirming option B. The passage does not state that the Supreme Court sanctioned any lawyers in this specific case, only that it set aside the order.

questions.q: The passage's closing paragraph draws a connection between this ruling and India's approach at the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance. What is that connection?
options: Both reflect India developing AI-era rules gradually, case by case or through guidelines, rather than via one comprehensive law.
Both events resulted in a formal ban on generative AI in India.
The Geneva dialogue directly overturned the Supreme Court's ruling.
India adopted the EU's AI Act as a result of the Geneva dialogue.
questions.explain: The passage explicitly frames both as evidence of India building AI-era rules 'case by case... rather than through one sweeping statute' — option A restates this directly. The other options assert events the passage does not describe.

questions.q: The European Union's AI Act, mentioned as a contrasting regulatory model, is best characterised as which kind of framework?
options: A voluntary, non-binding set of guidelines
A risk-tiered regulation imposing stricter obligations on higher-risk AI systems
A treaty binding only on AI companies headquartered in the US
A framework focused exclusively on AI in judicial proceedings
questions.explain: This draws on outside knowledge: the EU AI Act (2024) classifies AI systems by risk level, with the strictest compliance obligations for 'high-risk' uses — the passage gestures at this as 'a lighter regulatory touch than the European Union has chosen' without spelling out the Act's actual structure.

passages.title: Chairing a table that keeps getting bigger
passages.passage:
India took over the BRICS chairmanship on 1 January 2026 for the fourth time, having previously held the role in 2012, 2016, and 2021. The grouping that India now chairs bears only a loose resemblance to the one Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill described in 2001, when he coined "BRIC" to describe Brazil, Russia, India, and China as the emerging economies he expected to reshape global growth. South Africa joined in 2010, and the 2023 Johannesburg summit expanded the bloc sharply further, admitting Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. With Indonesia's later accession, BRICS now counts eleven full members, together accounting for close to half the world's population.

That expansion has made India's hosting year considerably more complicated than its earlier turns at the chair. BRICS today includes Iran, at war with the United States and Israel through much of 2026, and Russia, still fighting in Ukraine — two members India must accommodate at the same summit table while maintaining a foreign policy that has neither joined Western sanctions on either country nor endorsed their positions outright. It is a balancing act India has practised for years in its bilateral relationships; BRICS simply requires performing it multilaterally, in front of ten other governments simultaneously.

The year's groundwork runs through dozens of sectoral meetings feeding into September's leaders' summit in New Delhi — India hosted the eleventh BRICS Energy Ministers' Meeting in Gurugram in late June, one of several ministerial tracks alongside finance, trade, and health. The bloc's own development bank, the New Development Bank, headquartered in Shanghai since 2014, offers member states financing without the conditions Western-led institutions are often accused of attaching — part of what gives BRICS its appeal to member states wary of a global financial architecture still shaped mostly by the G7's postwar priorities.

Whether a grouping this large, holding members with actively opposed interests on some of the year's biggest conflicts, can still produce a meaningful joint communique in September is the real test of India's chairmanship — a test earlier, smaller BRICS summits never quite had to face.

questions.q: What is the main argument the passage develops about India's 2026 BRICS chairmanship?
options: India's chairmanship is a formality with no real diplomatic challenge.
The bloc's expansion has made India's hosting year more complicated, since it must now balance member states with directly opposed interests in ongoing conflicts.
BRICS should exclude Iran and Russia from future summits.
The New Development Bank has replaced the World Bank entirely.
questions.explain: The passage's second paragraph makes this the explicit turning point of its argument. Option D overstates the NDB's role; the passage frames it as an alternative source of financing, not a replacement for the World Bank.

questions.q: What can be inferred about why the passage calls India's approach to Iran and Russia within BRICS an extension of a 'balancing act it has practised for years'?
options: India has historically avoided all foreign relationships with conflict-involved states.
India has long managed bilateral relationships with countries in conflict with each other without fully aligning with either side, and BRICS now requires doing this in a multilateral setting.
India only began this balancing approach in 2023 after the Johannesburg expansion.
BRICS membership requires all countries to take identical foreign policy positions.
questions.explain: The passage explicitly frames this as a bilateral skill India now must exercise 'multilaterally, in front of ten other governments simultaneously' — implying continuity with, not a break from, past practice. Option C wrongly dates the practice's origin to 2023.

questions.q: According to the passage, which of the following is TRUE about the 2023 Johannesburg summit?
options: It resulted in South Africa joining BRICS for the first time.
It admitted Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE to the bloc.
It was the summit where India first chaired BRICS.
It reduced BRICS's membership from eleven to five.
questions.explain: The passage states this directly. South Africa's accession happened earlier, in 2010, not at Johannesburg — a common trap pairing the wrong expansion event with the wrong country.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest is the appeal of the New Development Bank to some BRICS member states?
options: It offers lower interest rates than any other global lender.
It offers financing without the conditions Western-led institutions are often accused of attaching.
It is legally required to lend only to BRICS founding members.
It replaced the IMF as the world's primary currency-stabilisation body.
questions.explain: The passage states this explicitly as the NDB's appeal. The other options describe claims the passage never makes about the NDB's interest rates, lending restrictions, or role relative to the IMF.

questions.q: The passage describes BRICS's combined population share but not its combined share of global GDP. Based on general knowledge of the bloc's economic weight, which figure is most commonly cited for BRICS's share of global GDP?
options: Around 10%
Around 25%
Around 40%
Around 75%
questions.explain: This draws on outside static knowledge commonly cited in BRICS coverage: the bloc's members together account for roughly 40% of global GDP, a figure the passage does not state but which a well-prepared aspirant should know independently.

passages.title: A bigger tournament crowns a familiar name
passages.passage:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup was, by design, a bigger tournament than any before it — the first played with 48 teams rather than 32, spread across sixteen cities in three host nations, Canada, Mexico, and the United States. Mexico opened the tournament on 11 June at the Estadio Azteca, a stadium already carrying the distinction of hosting World Cup finals in 1970 and 1986, long before it took on a third World Cup's opening match rather than its climax.

The expanded format changed which teams got to experience the tournament's later rounds. Egypt reached a World Cup knockout stage for the first time in the country's history, eliminating Australia on penalties — a result that would have been impossible in the older 32-team format, where Egypt's group might simply not have produced a qualifier. Whether a bigger tournament dilutes quality or widens opportunity was a debate that ran through the group stage; Egypt's run offered the strongest answer for the "widens opportunity" side.

None of that changed who eventually lifted the trophy. Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the final at New York/New Jersey Stadium, Ferran Torres scoring the only goal in front of more than 80,000 spectators. It was Spain's second men's title, following 2010, and because Spain's women's team already held the Women's World Cup, the win made Spain the first nation to hold both titles simultaneously — a genuine first, not a repeated fact dressed up as one.

Individual honours went to France's Kylian Mbappé, whose ten goals won him the Golden Boot and made him football's all-time leading World Cup scorer, surpassing a record that had stood since 2014. Total attendance crossed roughly seven million across the tournament, a new record for the competition — proof, if proof were needed, that a bigger World Cup drew a bigger audience, even if it did not obviously produce better football.

questions.q: What is the main idea the passage conveys about the 2026 World Cup's expanded format?
options: The 48-team format definitively produced worse football than the 32-team format.
The expanded format widened opportunity for teams like Egypt to reach the knockout stage, even as the eventual champion remained a traditional footballing power.
The expanded format was cancelled midway through the tournament.
Only European teams benefited from the expanded format.
questions.explain: The passage presents Egypt's run as evidence for the 'widens opportunity' side of the debate while noting the final still featured Spain and Argentina, two traditional powers — option B captures both threads. Option A overstates a debate the passage leaves open, not resolved.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the passage's mention that Egypt's result 'would have been impossible in the older 32-team format'?
options: Egypt has never previously qualified for a World Cup.
The larger format likely improved lower-ranked teams' statistical chances of advancing past the group stage.
The 32-team format did not include an Africa qualification spot.
Egypt was disqualified from all previous World Cups.
questions.explain: The inference is about probability and format mechanics — more teams and more advancing slots (including third-place qualifiers) statistically improve a mid-table team's chances, without the passage claiming anything about Egypt's qualification history in earlier editions.

questions.q: According to the passage, which of these statements about the final is FALSE?
options: The final was decided in extra time.
Ferran Torres scored the winning goal.
The final was held at the Estadio Azteca.
More than 80,000 spectators attended the final.
questions.explain: The passage states the final was held at New York/New Jersey Stadium, not the Estadio Azteca — the Azteca hosted the opening match. This is the false statement the question asks for.

questions.q: Why does the passage describe Spain's men's-and-women's title double as 'a genuine first, not a repeated fact dressed up as one'?
options: Because no country had previously won both titles in the same historical period, making this the first time one nation held both simultaneously.
Because Spain had won both titles once before, in 2010.
Because the phrase refers to Spain's repeat win of the men's title alone.
Because the women's World Cup was held for the first time in 2026.
questions.explain: The phrasing distinguishes a genuinely new achievement (first simultaneous double) from something that might sound impressive but is actually a repetition of an earlier fact — the passage confirms this is the former, a first, not a repeat.

questions.q: The passage notes Mbappé's record 'had stood since 2014' without naming who held it. Based on general football knowledge, whose record did Mbappé surpass?
options: Pelé's
Miroslav Klose's
Diego Maradona's
Ronaldo Nazário's
questions.explain: This draws on outside knowledge: Germany's Miroslav Klose held the record for most career World Cup goals, set at the 2014 tournament, until Mbappé's 2026 tally surpassed it — a fact the passage gestures at without naming.
